answer: Yes. Pipe the output through the `display` piped command with the `commands` mode: `<command> | display <mode>`. The `commands` mode displays the configuration as CLI 'set' and 'add' commands, and is specifically intended for creating CLI scripts from the current configuration. To capture the whole node, use the recursive show: `show -r | display commands`. Other supported modes for the show command are list (the default display mode, one value per line), table, csv, keys-table, single-table, only-values (useful for script building), xml, json, xpath, and interactive (JSON in the 'jless' viewer; press 'q' or CTRL-C to leave, ':help' for help). `display -h` shows help.

Yes. Combine the `begin` and `until` piped commands. `<command> | begin <words>` displays the output of the previous command starting from a specified word, and the output begins with the line that matches the word. `<command> | until <words>` displays the output ending at a specified word, and the output ends with the line that matches the word. The guide states explicitly that begin can be used together with the until piped command to retrieve a sub-set of an output, and vice versa. For both, <words> is the line to begin with or end with, and it may contain spaces if enclosed in quotes. Examples: `show | begin ne-location` and `show | until ne-location`. Each also accepts -h for help.

Yes, use the `more` piped command, and position matters: multiple piped commands can be used sequentially, but `more` needs to be the last one in the command line. Syntax is `<command> | more [-h]`, where <command> is any display command such as tree or show. The page size matches exactly the size of the CLI session window, so it follows the terminal size, except on the serial port where the terminal size is fixed. When the page limit is reached the display pauses; press any key to resume, or [CTRL]+[C] to terminate the display and return to the prompt. <enter> shows the next line, while any other key (including <space> or <tab>) shows the next page. Example: `tree | include led | more`.

It does not fail. With the `sort` piped command, if an unrecognized attribute name is used it is simply ignored. Syntax is `<show command> | sort [-i] [<attribute>*]`, plus `| sort [-h]` for help. <attribute> is any attribute name that exists in the context of the output, and a list of attributes can be provided as parameters to sort by. To flip the order, use -i, which inverts the order in the output and can be used on its own or together with an attribute list. Sort without parameters displays the output sorted by object instance, the same as the default display. Examples: `show card | sort`, `show port | sort port-type`, `show user | sort -i user-group last-login-date`, and `show odu | sort -i`.

Capitalisation does not matter, and yes, patterns are supported. The `exclude` piped command filters out the lines that contain the given word or string: `<command> | exclude <filter>`, with `exclude -h` for help. The <filter> does a case insensitive comparison, so `show | exclude abc` and `show | exclude ABC` are equivalent. The filter supports regex (regular expressions), and it may be multiple words separated by spaces if enclosed by quotes, e.g. `show | exclude 'ne oper'`. Multiple piped commands can be used in a single command. Examples: `show | exclude ne` and `show led | exclude status`. The inverse commands are `include` and `grep`, which filter the output that includes the filtering text.

Use the `highlight` piped command, which visually marks up a word or set of words in the output of the previous command: `<command> | highlight <word> [<word>]`, with `highlight -h` for help. More than one word can be provided. The quoting is what distinguishes the two cases: words given without quotes are searched for separately, while words enclosed within quotes are searched for as a sentence, so a whole phrase must be quoted. <word> is any word to highlight and may contain spaces if enclosed by quotes. Examples: `show odu | highlight odu4` for one word, `show odu | highlight odu4 oduflex` for two separate words, and `show odu | highlight 'idle lower-layer-down' odu4` to highlight the sequence of words 'idle lower-layer-down' plus the word 'odu4'.

Yes, use the `linenum` piped command, which adds line numbers to the output of the previous command. Syntax is `<command> | linenum`, with `<command> | linenum -h` for help. It takes no other parameters; <command> is any display command such as tree or show. Example: `show | linenum` displays an output with enumerated lines. If you are already filtering with `grep`, that command has its own -n option, which displays line numbers in the result, alongside -a=<n> (lines of context after the match) and -b=<n> (lines of context before the match).
